pos: n. (Siricius, bishop of Rome 384–399, author of the earliest surviving papal decretal)
etymology: Latin Siricius, probably from Greek Seirios, scorching, the dog-star.
biblical_def: Siricius succeeded Damasus as bishop of Rome in 384. His pontificate is remembered for one document and one policy. The document is his letter of February 385 to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona, answering fifteen questions of discipline; it is the earliest surviving papal decretal, and its form — a Roman reply issued as binding law for a distant province, in the language of imperial rescripts — established the instrument by which the medieval papacy would legislate. The policy is clerical continence: Siricius required that bishops, priests, and deacons abstain from marital relations, and treated those who did not as violators of law. He also condemned Jovinian, who had argued that marriage and virginity are of equal honour. 1Ti 3:2 is the apostolic qualification his policy sits against, that a bishop be “the husband of one wife” (1Ti 3:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a decretal as a letter of the pope determining some point of ecclesiastical law, and celibacy as an unmarried state.
webster_full: DECRE'TAL, n. A letter of the pope, determining some point or question in ecclesiastical law; a book of decrees or edicts; a collection of the pope's decrees.
CEL'IBACY, n. An unmarried state; a single life; as the celibacy of priests.
CONTI'NENCE, n. Restraint; self-command; forbearance of lawful pleasure.
scriptures: A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach;
Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving of them which believe and know the truth.
Tit 1:5
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
Mat 23:9
And call no man your father upon the earth: for one is your Father, which is in heaven.
corruption_summary: The first papal decretal, and the first Roman law requiring clerical continence.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary names the celibacy requirement as corruption, on the plainest exegetical ground available. 1Ti 3:2 lists among a bishop's qualifications that he be the husband of one wife, and Tit 1:5 and the verse following repeat it for elders; an office whose qualification presumes marriage cannot have abstinence from marriage imposed as its condition. 1Ti 4:1 and 1Ti 4:3 go further and attach a characterisation to the practice, naming among the marks of apostasy those “Forbidding to marry” (1Ti 4:3).

The decretal form is the second and larger corruption, because it is the engine of the others. A letter from one bishop answering another's questions is ordinary counsel; a letter issued in the style of an imperial rescript, claiming to bind a province that had not asked Rome to legislate for it, is a claim of jurisdiction. Mat 23:9 forbids the honorific that came with it, “call no man your father upon the earth” (Mat 23:9). What is honourable in Siricius is his insistence on the Nicene faith and his opposition to real laxity; what the Reformation called the church away from began in instruments like his.
roots_summary: Greek episkopos (G1985), overseer, bishop; koluo (G2967), to forbid; gameo (G1060), to marry.
usage: “the husband of one wife” (1Ti 3:2) — the qualification his law contradicts.
“Forbidding to marry” (1Ti 4:3) — the characterisation Paul attaches.
“call no man your father upon the earth” (Mat 23:9) — the honorific of the new jurisdiction.

pos: n. (Celestine I, bishop of Rome 422–432, supporter of Cyril against Nestorius and opponent of Pelagianism)
biblical_def: Celestine I held the Roman see for a decade in which two doctrinal questions were settled for the whole church. On the first he was firmly right. When Nestorius of Constantinople began teaching that the Virgin should not be called Theotokos and so divided the Person of Christ, Celestine held a Roman synod in 430, condemned the teaching, and commissioned Cyril of Alexandria to execute the sentence; the Council of Ephesus in 431 confirmed it. On the second he was also right: he supported the African bishops against the Pelagian account of grace, and the Capitula Caelestini appended to his letters became a standard collection of Augustinian texts on grace used for centuries. He also sent Palladius as first bishop to the Irish. Eph 2:8 is the doctrine he defended against Pelagius, that grace is “the gift of God” (Eph 2:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a council as an assembly of prelates to consult on matters of religion, and heresy as a fundamental error in religion.
webster_full: COUN'CIL, n. An assembly of men summoned or convened for consultation, deliberation and advice; an assembly of prelates and doctors, convened for regulating matters of doctrine and discipline.
HER'ESY, n. A fundamental error in religion, or an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine of religion.
GRACE, n. The free unmerited love and favor of God, the spring and source of all the benefits men receive from him.
scriptures: Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Rom 5:12
Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned:
Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.
corruption_summary: He got Christ's Person and the doctrine of grace right, and used both to enlarge Rome's jurisdiction.
corruption_paragraphs: Celestine's doctrinal record is one the dictionary affirms without reserve. The unity of Christ's Person against Nestorius and the sovereignty of grace against Pelagius are two of the four or five questions on which the whole gospel turns, and he was on the right side of both when much of the Eastern episcopate was not. Rom 5:12 and Eph 2:8 are the texts; the Capitula preserved them in a usable form for the Latin church through the centuries when they were most neglected.

The corruption is the use made of being right. Celestine's letters to the Africans in the Apiarius affair claimed a Roman right to hear appeals from African clergy, which the Council of Carthage denied on the ground that the canons cited were not Nicene; the same claim that had failed under Zosimus was pressed again. Mat 16:18 is the text the claim was built on, and it names Christ as the builder of His church, not a successor as its proprietor. Gal 1:8 shows the apostolic method of settling doctrine: the gospel judges the messenger, including an angel from heaven, and so including a bishop of Rome.
usage: “it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8) — against Pelagius, rightly.
“as by one man sin entered into the world” (Rom 5:12) — the Augustinian ground he kept.
“upon this rock I will build my church” (Mat 16:18) — Christ the builder, not an heir.

pos: n. (Hormisdas, bishop of Rome 514–523, author of the formula that ended the Acacian schism)
etymology: Persian Hormizd, the name of the god Ahura Mazda, borne by a Persian family settled at Rome.
biblical_def: Hormisdas brought to an end the Acacian schism, the thirty-five-year breach between Rome and Constantinople that had followed the Henotikon of the emperor Zeno. In 519, when Justin I came to the throne wanting reunion, Hormisdas required that the Eastern bishops subscribe a written formula: it affirmed the Chalcedonian definition and the Tome of Leo, anathematised Nestorius, Eutyches, Dioscorus, and Acacius by name, and declared that the apostolic see had always kept the catholic faith unspotted and that communion with it was the test of orthodoxy. Some two thousand five hundred Eastern bishops eventually subscribed. The Chalcedonian half of the formula is right; the clause about Rome's unfailing fidelity was quoted at the First Vatican Council thirteen centuries later in support of papal infallibility. Eph 2:20 names the actual foundation.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a schism as a division or separation in a church, and a formula as a prescribed form, a set form of words.
webster_full: SCHISM, n. In a general sense, division or separation; but appropriately, a division or separation in a church or denomination of Christians.
FOR'MULA, n. A prescribed form; a rule or model; in church affairs, a confession of faith; as the formula of Concord.
SUBSCRIP'TION, n. The act of subscribing or writing one's name underneath; attestation by signature.
scriptures: Eph 2:20
And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone;
But if I tarry long, that thou mayest know how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.
Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
Mat 23:9
And call no man your father upon the earth: for one is your Father, which is in heaven.
corruption_summary: A formula that restored Chalcedonian orthodoxy in the East and claimed Rome had never erred.
corruption_paragraphs: The reunion of 519 was a real doctrinal gain, and the dictionary says so. The Henotikon had been an imperial attempt to secure peace by leaving the Chalcedonian definition vague, and vagueness about the two natures of Christ is not peace; Hormisdas required the definition and the Tome of Leo in writing, by name, and got them. Gal 1:8 is the standard he applied, that the gospel is not negotiable for the sake of communion.

The corruption is the clause about the apostolic see. A document that makes communion with one bishop the test of orthodoxy has changed the test, and the claim that the Roman church had always kept the faith unspotted was falsifiable when it was written and was falsified within a century and a half by Vigilius and Honorius. Eph 2:20 puts the church on the foundation of “the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone” (Eph 2:20) — the apostolic writings, not an apostolic office with heirs. 1Ti 3:15 makes the church the pillar and ground of the truth, which is a custodian's title: a pillar holds a weight it did not make.
roots_summary: Greek themelios (G2310), foundation; akrogoniaios (G204), chief corner stone; stulos (G4769), a pillar.
usage: “Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone” (Eph 2:20) — the actual foundation.
“the pillar and ground of the truth” (1Ti 3:15) — a custodian's title.
“let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8) — the standard he rightly applied in the East.

pos: n. (Agapetus I, bishop of Rome 535–536, who deposed the Monophysite patriarch of Constantinople and died there)
biblical_def: Agapetus I held the Roman see for less than a year and spent most of it in Constantinople. Sent east by the Ostrogothic king Theodahad on a political errand, he found that Anthimus, a Monophysite, had been installed as patriarch of Constantinople through the influence of the empress Theodora. Agapetus refused communion with him and refused to be moved by the emperor Justinian's pressure or the empress's. Anthimus was deposed, and Agapetus himself consecrated Mennas in his place, the only occasion on which a bishop of Rome consecrated a patriarch of Constantinople. He died in the capital in April 536. He had also planned, with Cassiodorus, a Christian library and school at Rome which the Gothic wars prevented. Act 5:29 is the ground he stood on before an emperor, “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a patriarch as a dignitary superior to archbishops, and to depose as to divest of office.
webster_full: PA'TRIARCH, n. In the Christian church, a dignitary superior to the order of archbishops; as the patriarch of Constantinople, of Alexandria, or of Antioch.
DEPOSE', v.t. To lay down; to divest of office; to dethrone; to degrade.
MONOPH'YSITE, n. One who maintains that Jesus Christ had but one nature, or that the divine and human nature were so united as to form only one nature.
scriptures: Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
Act 4:19
But Peter and John answered and said unto them, Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye.
Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.
corruption_summary: Eleven months as bishop of Rome, spent refusing an emperor and an empress over the two natures of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary honours Agapetus for the thing it honours in any churchman: he would not purchase imperial favour with a Christological concession. Theodora's patronage of the Monophysite party was the strongest force in Constantinople, and the practical course was to find a formula that let Anthimus keep the see. Act 4:19 puts the question he answered — whether it is right “in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God” (Act 4:19) — and 1Jn 4:1 requires the trying of spirits whoever is sponsoring them.

The doctrine at stake is the Chalcedonian definition, which the dictionary holds without reserve: one Person, two natures, divine and human, united without confusion, change, division, or separation. Monophysitism absorbs the humanity into the deity and so destroys the Mediator, since a Saviour who is not truly man has not obeyed or suffered as man. Gal 1:8 is the measure. The corruption to note in the episode is the one Agapetus himself exemplified in resisting it: that by the sixth century bishops of Rome travelled to Constantinople as agents of kings, and ecclesiastical questions were settled inside an imperial politics they could not escape.
roots_summary: Greek peitharcheo (G3980), to obey authority; dokimazo (G1381), to try; anathema (G331), accursed.
roots_lines: Greek peitharcheo (G3980) — to obey one in authority; Acts 5:29.
Greek enopion (G1799) — in the sight of; Acts 4:19.
usage: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29) — said in effect to Justinian.
“in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God” (Act 4:19) — the question.
“try the spirits whether they are of God” (1Jn 4:1) — whoever sponsors them.

pos: n. (Vigilius, bishop of Rome 537–555, who condemned, defended, and again condemned the Three Chapters under imperial pressure)
etymology: Latin vigilius, watchful, from vigil, awake, on watch.
biblical_def: Vigilius was installed in the Roman see in 537 after the deposition of Silverius, by the agency of Belisarius and with the empress Theodora's backing. His pontificate was consumed by the Three Chapters controversy. The emperor Justinian, seeking to conciliate the Monophysites, condemned the writings of Theodore of Mopsuestia, Theodoret, and Ibas; the Latin bishops held that condemning them undermined Chalcedon, which had received two of the three. Vigilius was brought to Constantinople and there, over nine years, issued a condemnation of the Chapters, withdrew it under Western protest, refused to attend the council of 553, was anathematised by it, and then submitted and confirmed its decrees. He died at Syracuse on the voyage home. 1Co 16:13 is the charge his career did not meet, to “stand fast in the faith” (1Co 16:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines vacillation as a wavering, and to recant as to retract a declaration or proposition.
webster_full: VACILLA'TION, n. A moving one way and the other; a wavering; fluctuation; inconstancy.
RECANT', v.t. To retract; to recall; to contradict a former declaration; to revoke a declaration or proposition.
ANATH'EMA, n. Excommunication with curses; a curse or denunciation by ecclesiastical authority.
scriptures: Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong.
Eph 4:14
That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive;
Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering; (for he is faithful that promised;)
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
corruption_summary: He condemned, retracted, refused, was anathematised, and submitted, on one question, over nine years.
corruption_paragraphs: Vigilius is the plainest historical refutation of the claim later built on the Formula of Hormisdas, that the Roman see has always kept the catholic faith unspotted. On a single doctrinal question he took, in sequence, the condemning position, the defending position, abstention, and the condemning position again, each change following a change in the pressure applied to him by an emperor who held him in the capital. Eph 4:14 describes the pattern exactly: men “tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine” (Eph 4:14).

The dictionary draws two conclusions. The first is doctrinal: Heb 10:23 requires that the profession of faith be held “without wavering” (Heb 10:23), and an office cannot supply that steadiness to a man who lacks it. The second is historical: the claim of an unfailing Roman judgment was advanced before the events that disprove it and has been maintained since in spite of them, which is why the Reformation treated the papal office itself, and not merely particular abuses, as the thing the church must be called away from. Act 5:29 is what Agapetus had said to the same emperor twenty years earlier, and Vigilius did not say it.
roots_summary: Greek steko (G4739), to stand fast; kludonizomai (G2831), to be tossed as by waves; aklines (G186), without wavering.
roots_lines: Greek kludonizomai (G2831) — to be tossed by waves; Ephesians 4:14.
usage: “stand fast in the faith” (1Co 16:13) — the charge not met.
“carried about with every wind of doctrine” (Eph 4:14) — nine years of it.
“hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering” (Heb 10:23) — the standard.

pos: n. (Pelagius II, bishop of Rome 579–590, who objected to the title of ecumenical patriarch and sent Gregory to Constantinople)
etymology: Greek pelagios, of the sea, from pelagos, the open sea; unrelated to the British heretic of the same name.
biblical_def: Pelagius II was elected in 579 while the Lombards were besieging Rome, and his pontificate was spent on two fronts. The first was survival: he sought help from Constantinople and, failing to get it, bought the Lombards off and turned to the Franks. He sent the deacon Gregory, afterwards Gregory the Great, as his representative to the imperial court, where Gregory spent six formative years. The second front was a title. When John IV of Constantinople, called the Faster, took or accepted the style of ecumenical patriarch, Pelagius objected and declared the acts of a synod held under it void — the beginning of the dispute Gregory would continue, calling the title a mark of the forerunner of antichrist. Mat 20:25 is the text the objection rested on, that dominion so exercised is the way of “the princes of the Gentiles” (Mat 20:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ecumenical as general, universal, and preeminence as superiority, the state of being the chief.
webster_full: ECUMEN'ICAL, a. General; universal; as an ecumenical council.
PREEM'INENCE, n. Superiority in degree; precedence; the state of being the chief or principal.
TI'TLE, n. An appellation of dignity, distinction or preeminence given to persons.
scriptures: But Jesus called them unto him, and said, Ye know that the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them, and they that are great exercise authority upon them.
But it shall not be so among you: but whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister;
I wrote unto the church: but Diotrephes, who loveth to have the preeminence among them, receiveth us not.
Mat 23:9
And call no man your father upon the earth: for one is your Father, which is in heaven.
corruption_summary: A bishop of Rome denounced the title of universal patriarch, and his successors took one just like it.
corruption_paragraphs: The irony here is the dictionary's whole point about the papal office, and it is not a cheap one. Pelagius II, and Gregory the Great after him, were right: a title claiming universal jurisdiction over the churches is contrary to Christ's express order for His ministers. Mat 20:26 states it as plainly as anything in the New Testament, that “it shall not be so among you” (Mat 20:26), and 3Jn 1:9 names the fault in a particular man, Diotrephes, “who loveth to have the preeminence among them” (3Jn 1:9).

Within two centuries the Roman see was claiming, by a more sweeping right than John the Faster had ever asserted, exactly what Pelagius had declared void in another. The dictionary holds that the argument of 579 was sound and that the Roman see is the chief defendant under it. Mat 23:9 forbids the title of father on earth; the papal office is built on both the title and the universal jurisdiction. The Lombard crisis is worth remembering alongside it: Pelagius died of plague in 590 with the city starving, and the man he had trained in Constantinople inherited all of it.
roots_summary: Greek katakurieuo (G2634), to lord over; diakonos (G1249), a servant; philoproteuo (G5383), to love preeminence.
roots_lines: Greek katakurieuo (G2634) — to exercise dominion over; Matthew 20:25.
Greek katexousiazo (G2715) — to exercise authority upon; Matthew 20:25.
Greek philoproteuo (G5383) — to love the first place; 3 John 9.
usage: “the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them” (Mat 20:25) — the objection's ground.
“it shall not be so among you” (Mat 20:26) — stated as plainly as anything.
“who loveth to have the preeminence among them” (3Jn 1:9) — named in a man.

pos: n. (Honorius I, bishop of Rome 625–638, condemned by name as a monothelite heretic by the Third Council of Constantinople)
biblical_def: Honorius I was an energetic administrator who repaired Roman churches, pressed the conversion of the English and the conformity of the Irish on Easter, and intervened in Spain. He is remembered for two letters. Sergius, patriarch of Constantinople, wrote to him about the formula then being used to conciliate the Monophysites, and Honorius replied endorsing the position that there is in Christ one will, and directing that the question of one or two operations not be pressed. Monothelitism is the doctrine those letters supported, and it is a denial of the Chalcedonian definition: a Christ with no human will has no complete human nature, and the obedience of Gethsemane and the cross is not the obedience of a man. The Third Council of Constantinople in 681 anathematised Honorius by name along with Sergius, and his successor Leo II confirmed the sentence. Gal 1:8 is the principle the council applied.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines will as the faculty by which we determine either to do or forbear an action, and anathema as excommunication with curses.
webster_full: WILL, n. That faculty or power of the mind by which we determine either to do or forbear an action.
ANATH'EMA, n. Excommunication with curses; a curse or denunciation by ecclesiastical authority, accompanying excommunication.
INFALLIBIL'ITY, n. The quality of being incapable of error or mistake; entire exemption from liability to error.
scriptures: Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.
Who opposeth and exalteth himself above all that is called God, or that is worshipped; so that he as God sitteth in the temple of God, shewing himself that he is God.
Eph 2:20
And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone;
corruption_summary: A bishop of Rome taught one will in Christ and was anathematised by name by an ecumenical council and by his own successor.
corruption_paragraphs: The doctrinal point first. The dictionary holds the Chalcedonian definition: one Person in two natures, divine and human, without confusion, change, division, or separation, and a complete human nature includes a human will. Monothelitism makes the Saviour's human nature incomplete, and with it the active obedience by which He fulfilled the law for His people; Gethsemane becomes a performance rather than a submission. 1Jn 4:1 and Gal 1:8 are the instruments the council used, and it used them on a bishop of Rome.

The historical point is the one the Reformation pressed and Rome has never answered. Honorius was condemned by name, in the acts of an ecumenical council Rome itself receives, and the condemnation was ratified by Pope Leo II; the claim of the Formula of Hormisdas and of the First Vatican Council cannot stand with it. The usual reply, that the letters were not formal definitions, concedes the substance, since the question put to Honorius was precisely a doctrinal question put to him as the one who should settle it. Eph 2:20 locates the church's foundation in the apostles and prophets with Christ the chief corner stone, and 2Th 2:4 describes an office that exalts itself in the temple of God — the text the Reformers applied to the papacy, and LBCF 26.4 names the pope antichrist on that ground.
roots_summary: Greek thelema (G2307), will; anathema (G331), accursed; huperairomai (G5229), to exalt oneself above.
roots_lines: Greek anathema (G331) — accursed, devoted to destruction; Galatians 1:8.
Greek euaggelizo (G2097) — to preach as good news; Galatians 1:8.
Greek huperairomai (G5229) — to exalt oneself above; 2 Thessalonians 2:4.
usage: “though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel” (Gal 1:8) — applied to a pope in 681.
“try the spirits whether they are of God” (1Jn 4:1) — the council's duty, and it tried him.
“exalteth himself above all that is called God” (2Th 2:4) — the Reformers' text on the office.

pos: n. (Martin I, bishop of Rome 649–655, condemner of monothelitism, arrested by the emperor and died in exile)
biblical_def: Martin I was elected in 649 without waiting for imperial confirmation, and within months he convened the Lateran Synod of that year, which condemned monothelitism, the imperial edicts that had protected it, and the patriarchs who taught it. Maximus the Confessor was the synod's theological force. The emperor Constans II had forbidden all discussion of the question by the edict called the Typos; Martin's synod discussed and defined it anyway. In 653 imperial troops arrested him in the Lateran, carried him to Constantinople, tried him on a charge of treason rather than of doctrine, and exiled him to Cherson in the Crimea, where he died in 655 of privation. He is the last bishop of Rome venerated as a martyr. Act 5:29 is the sentence his arrest and death enforce, “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a synod as an ecclesiastical council, and exile as banishment from one's country.
webster_full: SYN'OD, n. A council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion; an ecclesiastical council.
EX'ILE, n. The state of being banished from one's country; banishment; the person banished.
CONFES'SOR, n. One who makes a profession of his faith in the Christian religion; one who avows his religion in the face of danger.
scriptures: Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
Rev 2:10

Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.
They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword: they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented;
Mat 5:10
Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
corruption_summary: He defined the doctrine an emperor had forbidden anyone to discuss, and died for it in the Crimea.
corruption_paragraphs: Martin's case is the exact counterpart of Honorius's, and the dictionary sets them side by side deliberately. On the same question, one bishop of Rome endorsed the error under imperial pressure and another defined the truth against imperial prohibition and died of it. Whatever else that proves, it proves that the see supplies no guarantee: the men differ, and the doctrine has to be judged by Scripture in either case. Rev 2:10 is the promise Martin received, “be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life” (Rev 2:10).

The Typos is worth naming as a species of corruption that recurs in every age: an authority which cannot win a doctrinal argument forbids the argument, and calls the prohibition peace. Martin and Maximus both refused the silence and both were mutilated or exiled for it. Heb 11:37 lists what such men have suffered, and Mat 5:10 pronounces the blessing. The dictionary honours Martin without granting the office he held, in just the way it honours Gregory the Great's pastoral instincts: fidelity in a man is one thing and the claims of his see are another.
roots_summary: Greek peitharcheo (G3980), to obey authority; stephanos (G4735), a crown; dioko (G1377), to persecute.
roots_lines: Greek peitharcheo (G3980) — to obey one in authority; Acts 5:29.
usage: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29) — against the Typos.
“be thou faithful unto death” (Rev 2:10) — Cherson, 655.
“Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake” (Mat 5:10) — the verdict on him.

pos: n. (Sergius I, bishop of Rome 687–701, who refused the Quinisext canons and sent Willibrord to the Frisians)
etymology: Latin Sergius, a Roman gens name of Etruscan origin.
biblical_def: Sergius I was a Syrian by descent, born at Palermo, and reached the Roman see in 687 after a disputed election. Two acts define his pontificate. The first was a refusal: when the emperor Justinian II sent him the canons of the Quinisext Council of 692 for subscription, Sergius declined to sign, because the canons legislated on Western usages — clerical marriage, the Saturday fast, the representation of Christ as a lamb — and placed Constantinople's rank beside Rome's. Imperial troops were sent to arrest him and the militia of Ravenna prevented it. The second was missionary: he baptized Caedwalla the West Saxon king at Rome, consecrated Willibrord bishop for the Frisians in 695, and encouraged the English mission to the continent. Mar 16:15 is the commission the second act served, to “preach the gospel to every creature” (Mar 16:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a canon as a law or rule of doctrine or discipline, and a council as an assembly convened for regulating matters of doctrine and discipline.
webster_full: CAN'ON, n. In an ecclesiastical sense, a law or rule of doctrine or discipline, enacted by a council and confirmed by the sovereign.
COUN'CIL, n. An assembly of prelates and doctors, convened for regulating matters of doctrine and discipline.
MIS'SION, n. A being sent or delegated by authority, with certain powers for transacting business.
scriptures: And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.
Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
Act 1:8

But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.
What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it.
corruption_summary: He would not sign a council's canons and did sign a missionary bishop's commission.
corruption_paragraphs: The Quinisext refusal is instructive on both sides. Sergius was right that a council sitting at Constantinople had no warrant to legislate the discipline of churches that had not sent delegates, and some of the canons he objected to — those permitting the marriage of priests and deacons — were nearer the New Testament than the Roman rule he was defending, which is an irony the dictionary notes rather than conceals. The underlying question is the one Deu 12:32 raises for all such legislation: what is added to what God commanded, and by whose authority.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the second half of his record. Sergius consecrated Willibrord for the Frisians and backed the English mission to the continent, and that chain — Rome to the English, the English to the Frisians and the Germans, and through Boniface to the Carolingian church — is how northern Europe was evangelised. Mat 28:19 and Act 1:8 are the commission; a bishop who spends his energies on canonical precedence and none on sending men is of less use than one who does both, and Sergius did both.
roots_summary: Greek ktisis (G2937), creature; matheteuo (G3100), to make disciples; Hebrew yacaph (H3254), to add.
usage: “preach the gospel to every creature” (Mar 16:15) — Willibrord to the Frisians.
“Go ye therefore, and teach all nations” (Mat 28:19) — the chain to the Germans.
“thou shalt not add thereto” (Deu 12:32) — the question under every canon.

pos: n. (Anastasius the Librarian, c. 810–878, archivist of the Roman church and chief Latin translator of Greek conciliar and patristic texts)
etymology: Greek anastasis, resurrection; Latin bibliothecarius, a librarian, from bibliotheca, a library.
biblical_def: Anastasius Bibliothecarius was a Roman clerk of great learning and a turbulent career: set up as a rival claimant to the Roman see in 855 and excommunicated for it, he was restored, and from about 867 served as librarian and chancellor of the Roman church under four bishops of Rome. His value is as a translator. Almost alone in the Latin West of his century he read Greek well, and he rendered into Latin the acts of the Seventh and Eighth Councils, the works of Dionysius and of Maximus the Confessor, lives of the Greek fathers, and the Chronographia tripertita, a compilation of Byzantine chronicles. For centuries the Latin church knew much of the Greek conciliar record only through him, and he took part in the negotiations over Photius and over the mission of Cyril and Methodius. Pro 18:15 describes his working life, that “The heart of the prudent getteth knowledge” (Pro 18:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a librarian as the keeper of a library, and a translator as one who renders into another language.
webster_full: LIBRA'RIAN, n. The keeper or one who has the care of a library or collection of books.
TRANSLA'TOR, n. One who renders into another language; one who expresses the sense of words in one language by equivalent words in another.
AR'CHIVES, n. The place in which records are kept; records or ancient writings preserved.
scriptures: The heart of the prudent getteth knowledge; and the ear of the wise seeketh knowledge.
Psa 78:4
We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done.
And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
corruption_summary: A disgraced antipope became the one man in the Latin West who could read the Greek councils.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary records Anastasius's history without softening it: he was intruded into the Roman see as a rival claimant, excommunicated, deposed, and afterwards rehabilitated and employed. It is a mark of how little the ninth-century papacy could afford to lose a man who knew Greek. The value of his labour is nonetheless real and lasting, and Psa 78:4 names the principle it served, that the record not be hidden from the children.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the standing of translation and archive-keeping among the church's necessary works. Without Anastasius the Latin Middle Ages would have had almost no access to the acts of the councils they appealed to, and the Reformers' own recovery of the patristic witness rested on manuscript traditions men like him preserved. 2Ti 2:15 commends the workman rightly dividing the word, and Luk 24:27 shows the end for which every such labour exists — the expounding of “the things concerning himself” (Luk 24:27) out of all the scriptures.
roots_summary: Hebrew bin (H995), to discern; kachad (H3582), to hide; Greek diermeneuo (G1329), to expound.
roots_lines: Hebrew bin (H995) — to discern, be prudent; Proverbs 18:15.
usage: “The heart of the prudent getteth knowledge” (Pro 18:15) — forty years in an archive.
“We will not hide them from their children” (Psa 78:4) — what translation preserves.
“the things concerning himself” (Luk 24:27) — the end of every such labour.
